explanation: SET NOCOUNT OFF makes the procedure send row-count messages in addition to its result sets.
With XACT_ABORT OFF, a run-time error can abort only the failing statement and leave an explicit transaction open.
@CustomerIdText fixes the customer identifier at N'1' instead of using the supplied @CustomerID.
@OrderID starts with an unexplained order identifier of 1, which can survive a later assignment if the query returns no rows.
SELECT * returns every Sales.Orders column, including its large text fields, and makes the result shape depend on the table schema.
No ORDER BY defines which ten OrderIDs are returned.
Sales.Orders.OrderID is the primary key, so DISTINCT cannot remove any duplicates.
NOLOCK can return uncommitted OrderIDs or miss or repeat rows during concurrent changes.
YEAR(o.OrderDate) tests a computed year instead of exposing a date range that could be sought directly.
The order filter fixes the reporting year at 2016.
CustomerID is int, so SQL Server must convert the nvarchar variable @CustomerIdText to int for the comparison.
The OR combines an unrestricted scan for NULL with a selective CustomerID lookup; one cached plan may not suit both cases.
The initial % in N'%urgent%' requires a substring search of Comments rather than a prefix lookup.
The word 'urgent' is embedded as the criterion for selecting orders by comment.
ISNULL wraps the indexed Orders.CustomerID even though it is NOT NULL; a direct key comparison needs no such expression.
The ISNULL fallback assigns 0 an undocumented meaning as a substitute customer identifier.
The equality test selects the fixed customer identifier 1 instead of @CustomerID.
Adding zero to OrderID changes a direct primary-key lookup into a comparison against an arithmetic expression.
CustomerID <> 1 can qualify orders for nearly every customer rather than targeting a selective key range.
Customer identifier 1 is embedded as a special exclusion.
TOP (1) chooses an unspecified order/customer pair from the cross join.
CROSS JOIN pairs each order with every customer, so the returned customer need not own the order.
No ordering determines which matching order/line row supplies the single OrderID.
Orders and OrderLines are comma-separated, leaving their OrderID join condition mixed into the WHERE clause.
The scalar line count depends on the outer OrderID and can require a separate OrderLines lookup for each order.
The EXISTS test is correlated on o.OrderID and can probe OrderLines per order. A join to the distinct qualifying OrderIDs would preserve the existence semantics.
The qualifying order-line quantity threshold is fixed at greater than 1.
ORDER BY repeats the Comments CASE expression even though the same value is available as HasComments.
ORDER BY 2 means OrderDate only while OrderDate remains the second select-list column.
Orders can share OrderDate, so the page boundary is unstable without a unique tie-breaker such as OrderID.
The first UNION branch selects the fixed order identifier 1.
The branches select different primary-key values, so neither within-branch nor cross-branch duplicates require UNION's duplicate removal.
The second UNION branch selects the fixed order identifier 2.
The scalar subquery references the current o.OrderID, so finding qualifying orders can require repeated probes into OrderLines.
COUNT(*) > 0 requests the number of matching lines even though the first matching line answers the test.
Multiple orders overwrite @OrderID in unspecified order, while an empty result leaves its previous value unchanged.
No ORDER BY determines which five OrderIDs are inserted into @OrderIds.
The five orders copied into #ImplicitOrders depend on the access order, not a defined selection order.
SELECT INTO derives the schema of #ImplicitOrders from the projection instead of declaring its columns and constraints explicitly.
order_cursor is opened and fetched just once to assign an unordered OrderID; cursor setup and teardown are unnecessary for a single scalar lookup.
Converting @CustomerID to text embeds the ID in the statement, changing the batch text for each value; a NULL ID can also null out the batch.
EXEC runs the constructed CustomerID lookup with no bound input parameter.
Appending the text of @OrderID produces different SQL text for different order identifiers.
sys.sp_executesql receives only @Sql, with no parameter declaration or bound OrderID.
#Scratch is explicitly created but never dropped, so the unused temp object remains until procedure-scope cleanup.
The CATCH returns ERROR_MESSAGE() as a normal result set without rethrowing or returning a failure status.
The negative-order-ID path uses RAISERROR rather than THROW; RAISERROR does not honor XACT_ABORT.
The procedure emits its diagnostic through PRINT, a potentially buffered message rather than a structured diagnostic.
The order lookup uses customer identifier 1 instead of the supplied @CustomerID.
The lower bound for OrderDate is the unexplained fixed date '20160101'.
Without a conversion style, '01/02/2016' can mean January 2 or February 1 depending on DATEFORMAT.
No ORDER BY defines which matching order/invoice row supplies the returned OrderID.
COALESCE wraps the indexed Orders.CustomerID join key even though that column is NOT NULL.
The Orders operand uses 0 as an undocumented substitute customer identifier.
The other COALESCE wraps the indexed Invoices.CustomerID join key, which is also NOT NULL.
The Invoices operand separately uses 0 as an undocumented substitute customer identifier.
TOP (1) returns an unspecified OrderID from the self-join.
Joining o2 on the same Orders primary key maps every order to itself without adding columns or filtering rows.
Sorting orders by the nvarchar(max) Comments column can require large text comparisons and substantial sort memory.
SUM(ol.Quantity) must account for every Sales.OrderLines row because there is no filter.
OrderID > 0 tests only the grouping key and can filter input rows in WHERE rather than groups in HAVING.
The result uses a fixed OrderID cutoff of 0, although the supplied key definition does not require positive IDs.
COUNT(*) requests the cardinality of all Sales.Orders rows without a restrictive predicate.
COUNT(*) without GROUP BY returns exactly one row, so ordering by OrderCount has no effect.
MERGE is used for a single matched update on OrderID, introducing MERGE-specific locking and correctness concerns for an operation expressible as UPDATE.
The matched action assigns target.Comments to itself; it can lock the row and fire update triggers without changing the value.
SET Comments = Comments performs an update on the selected order without changing its comment.
Deleting by Quantity alone can remove lines from unrelated orders; neither OrderLineID nor OrderID restricts the deletion.
The delete treats quantity -1 as a deletion marker without defining that business convention.
WAITFOR DELAY keeps the request and a worker waiting for one second on the write path.
The transaction and its unconditional rollback are outside TRY/CATCH. If a caller already has a transaction, the rollback can undo the caller's work too.
Sales.Orders has no IDENTITY column in the supplied DDL, so enabling IDENTITY_INSERT fails when this branch runs.
sp_who is invoked without its sys schema qualifier, leaving procedure resolution implicit.
ROWCOUNT 1 is not reset within the procedure, so subsequent queries and writes can silently return or affect only one row.
The category insert relies on the physical column order of #DemoCategories to map its ID and name.
The new category is assigned the fixed CategoryID 99 regardless of @NewCategory.
The four SELECT expressions map into #DemoCustomers by position because the INSERT omits its target columns.
Prepending '%' to @CustomerName prevents a prefix seek on the Sales.Customers customer-name index.
Raw @CustomerName text is inserted into a quoted SQL literal and then executed. The input can change the statement instead of remaining a LIKE parameter.
The dynamic batch is invoked through sp_executesql without the sys schema qualifier.
sp_executesql receives only the SQL text; there is no bound parameter for the customer-name pattern.
Every row in #DemoCustomers qualifies for the category change. ROWCOUNT limits how many rows can change, not which customer qualifies.
The update forces CustomerCategoryID to the fixed category identifier 1.
The WHERE comparison rejects NULL-extended Orders rows, so the LEFT JOIN cannot preserve customers without a qualifying order.
The order join result is restricted by an unexplained fixed cutoff of '2016-01-01'.
DeliveryMethodID = NULL cannot be true under ANSI NULL semantics. The supplied DeliveryMethodID column is also NOT NULL.
dbo.GetCustomerType is called in the projection and can execute once per customer unless SQL Server can inline it.
If the DELETE or COMMIT fails after BEGIN TRANSACTION, the CATCH never rolls back the outstanding transaction and can leave locks held.
Selecting ERROR_MESSAGE() does not propagate the transaction failure to the caller as an exception or failure status.
INDEX = 1 forces the clustered index on Sales.Customers, excluding alternative access paths such as its CustomerName index.
Three nested derived tables, t3, t2 and t1, merely pass CustomerID through from a name filter that needs only one SELECT.
The initial % in '%A%' prevents a prefix seek on the indexed CustomerName column.
The customer-name test uses the fixed search text 'A' rather than a supplied search term.
SELECT * exposes every column returned by dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti, coupling the procedure's result shape to the function's return schema.
The name GetCustomerOrdersMulti suggests a multi-statement TVF, which would materialize its result rather than expose the order query for inlining. The function definition is needed to confirm this.
